name: Charles Henry Morgan
bio: A South Carolina native, Charles Henry Morgan worked in Atlanta as a carriage trimmer before building a prosperous grocery business. He signed South-View's charter petition, bought three shares of its stock on December 6, 1886, and was buried there on December 17, 1886.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 3, "The Founders": "The Charter" and "Charles Henry Morgan"

name: George Wesley Graham
bio: George Wesley Graham, a carpenter, was elected in December 1870 as one of Atlanta's first two Black city council members and represented the Third Ward in 1871. He later ran a grocery and wood-and-coal business and signed South-View's 1886 charter petition.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 3, "The Founders": "The Charter" and "George Wesley Graham"

name: Rev. Robert Grant
bio: Born about 1826 in Wilkes County, Rev. Robert Grant was a blacksmith and drayman who became founding pastor of Atlanta's Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872. He signed South-View's 1886 charter petition and was buried there after his death in 1896.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 3, "The Founders": "The Charter" and "Robert Grant"

name: Albert Watts
bio: Albert Watts, a Clarke County native who ran a grocery on Fraser Street, signed South-View's 1886 charter petition and served as its first treasurer until his death in 1903. His son Lewis and grandson Albert Hawes Watts later led the cemetery association.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 3, "The Founders": "The Charter" and "Albert Watts" (also ch. 1 opening and Appendix entry "Watts, Albert")
Georgia Institute of Technology, Building Memories project, "South-View Cemetery" (Jacqueline Jones Royster, with Prachi Mehta)

name: Adrienne McNeil Herndon
bio: A Savannah native and Atlanta University graduate, Herndon taught elocution and drama there and staged the university's first Shakespeare production in 1905. In 1904 she made a Boston stage debut under the name Anne Du Bignon, and she designed the family's Herndon Home.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 6, "Herndon: Simplicity of Design"; also ch. 11, "A Litany of Atlanta", and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary", section H ("Herndon, Adrienne McNeil")

Atlanta History Center, "What Moves You?" exhibition, "Adrienne McNeil Herndon"

name: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner
bio: Born free in South Carolina, Turner served as a Union Army chaplain, helped build the AME Church in Georgia, and was elected to the Georgia legislature in 1868. Elected an AME bishop in 1880, he later championed emigration to Africa; about 25,000 mourners attended his 1915 Atlanta funeral.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 12, "Turner: A Noble and Indomitable Spirit"; also ch. 6, "A Beautiful Place for a Cemetery"
New Georgia Encyclopedia, Stephen Angell, "Henry McNeal Turner (1834-1915)"
South Carolina Encyclopedia (University of South Carolina), "Turner, Henry McNeal"
Georgia Historical Society, historical marker "South-View Cemetery" (2016)

name: Rev. John D. Render
bio: Rev. John D. Render, an AME minister who earned his living as a drayman, signed South-View's 1886 charter petition and bought two shares of its stock. He later helped charter the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company and served as a Morris Brown College trustee.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 3, "The Founders": "The Charter" and "John D. Render" (also ch. 4, "Early Leaders at South-View")

name: Alonzo F. Herndon
bio: Born into slavery in Walton County, Georgia, Herndon became a leading Atlanta barber and in 1905 bought a small mutual aid association that grew into the Atlanta Life Insurance Company. He also served as South-View's president and treasurer.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 6, "Herndon: Simplicity of Design"; also ch. 4, "Business Life on Auburn Avenue", and ch. 1, "The People"

name: Moses Amos
bio: Moses Amos learned the drug trade as a boy and managed Butler, Slater & Co., an early Black-owned Atlanta pharmacy. In 1911 he became the first African American licensed as a druggist by Georgia's pharmacy board, and in 1914 he opened the Gate City Drug Store in Auburn Avenue's Odd Fellows Building.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 13, "Genealogy in the Cemetery Landscape", section "Holmes-Amos: Family Tree in Stone"; also Biographical Dictionary entry "Amos, Moses"

name: David T. Howard
bio: Born enslaved in 1849, David T. Howard worked as a railroad porter before opening an Atlanta undertaking business in 1883. An original investor and board member of the South-View Cemetery Association, he donated the land for the school later named for him.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 5, "Caring for the Dead", section "David T. Howard"; also ch. 1, "The History" and "The People", and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary", H, "Howard, David T. Sr."

name: Alice Dugged Cary
bio: Educator Alice Dugged Cary became principal of Atlanta's Mitchell Street School in 1886, the city's first Black woman principal. In 1921 she became the first librarian of the Auburn Branch, Atlanta's first free public library for African Americans, and led it until 1929.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), "A Selected Biographical Dictionary", entry "Cary, Alice Dugged"

name: Rev. Edward R. Carter
bio: Carter was pastor of Atlanta's Friendship Baptist Church for about six decades and an original stockholder and board member of South-View. His 1894 book The Black Side records the businesses, churches, and schools of Black Atlanta.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 13, "Carter: 'A Noble Citizen, A Christian Gentleman'"; also ch. 1, "The History", and ch. 4, "South-View's Original Stockholders"

name: Benjamin Jefferson Davis Sr.
bio: Founder, editor and publisher of the Atlanta Independent, a Black weekly newspaper, and a leader of Georgia's Odd Fellows whose push helped build the Odd Fellows Building on Auburn Avenue. He was also active in Republican Party politics as a national committeeman.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 10, "Benjamin Jefferson Davis: Odd Fellows Grand Director"; appendix entry "Davis, Benjamin Jefferson"
National Park Service, National Register of Historic Places Inventory-Nomination Form, "Odd Fellows Building and Auditorium" (Atlanta, 1975)

name: 1st Lt. Walter Drake Westmoreland
bio: An Atlanta native who earned his pilot wings at Tuskegee in 1943, Westmoreland flew with the 332nd Fighter Group in World War II. He was shot down and killed over Hungary on October 13, 1944, returning from an escort mission to Blechhammer, Germany; his remains were later returned to Atlanta.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), A Selected Biographical Dictionary, "U - W" (entry "Westmoreland, Walter Drake"); also ch. 1, "Notable Residents of South-View's Historic Section"

name: John Wesley Dobbs
bio: John Wesley Dobbs worked 32 years as a railway mail clerk and led Georgia's Prince Hall Masons as Grand Master from 1932. Called the unofficial "mayor of Auburn Avenue," he coined the name "Sweet Auburn" and co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League in 1946.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 10, "Symbols of Fraternity and Benevolence": "Prince Hall Freemasonry" and "The Broken Column Monument"; also ch. 1, "Twentieth-Century Residents", and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary" (D)

name: Ludie Clay Andrews
bio: Trained at Spelman's MacVicar Hospital (1906), Ludie Andrews organized Grady Hospital's Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses in 1914 and, after a long legal fight with the state nursing board, became Georgia's first Black registered nurse. She led MacVicar Hospital from 1928 to 1948.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 1, "Historical Overview: A Cemetery of Their Own", section "Twentieth-Century Residents" (mention); and Biographical Dictionary entry "Andrews, Ludie Clay"

name: Irene Thompson Dobbs
bio: Irene Ophelia Thompson, a native of Columbus, Mississippi, married John Wesley Dobbs in 1906; all six of their daughters, including soprano Mattiwilda Dobbs, graduated from Spelman College. She chaired the deaconess board of First Congregational Church and served on the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA board.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), "A Selected Biographical Dictionary" (D), entry "Dobbs, John Wesley" (Irene Ophelia Thompson Dobbs is profiled within it)

name: Alberta Williams King
bio: The daughter of Ebenezer Baptist Church pastor A. D. Williams, she founded Ebenezer's choir and was its organist from 1932 to 1972. The mother of Martin Luther King Jr., she was shot and killed while playing the organ at a Sunday service on June 30, 1974.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), A Selected Biographical Dictionary, "I - K" (entry "Alberta Williams", under King, Martin Luther Sr.); also ch. 6, "Mausoleum Row"

name: Norris B. Herndon
bio: The only child of Alonzo and Adrienne Herndon, he earned a Harvard MBA in 1921 and led Atlanta Life Insurance Company as president from 1927 to 1973. He created the Herndon Foundation in 1950 and served as vice president and board chair of South-View.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 6, "Herndon: Simplicity of Design"; also ch. 4, "Business Life on Auburn Avenue", and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary", section H ("Herndon, Norris Bumstead")

name: Rev. Martin Luther King Sr.
bio: King was pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church for 44 years and an early civil rights leader in Atlanta's NAACP and Civic and Political League, leading a voter-registration march to City Hall and a campaign for equal pay for Black teachers. He was the father of Martin Luther King Jr.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), A Selected Biographical Dictionary, "I - K" (entry "King, Martin Luther Sr."); also ch. 6, "Mausoleum Row", and ch. 11, "Martin Luther King Jr."

name: Lorimer D. Milton
bio: Lorimer D. Milton led Citizens Trust Bank as president from 1938 until 1971 and co-owned the Yates and Milton drugstores; he also taught at Morehouse College. He served on the South-View Cemetery Association board, including as its first vice president.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), "A Selected Biographical Dictionary" (L - M), entry "Milton, Lorimer Douglas"; also ch. 4, "The Business of Death": "1960s - Seventy-Fifth Anniversary" and "1970s - Ninetieth Anniversary"; ch. 1, "The People" (memorial to board members)

name: Eldren M. Bailey
bio: A plasterer by trade, Eldren Bailey made whitewashed cement grave markers for Atlanta's Black funeral homes from the 1920s, many of them at South-View. From 1945 he filled the yard of his Rockwell Street home with self-taught cement and plaster sculptures.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 7, "Vernacular Memorial Traditions", section "The Gravestone Art of Eldren Bailey"

name: Grace Towns Hamilton
bio: Grace Towns Hamilton led the Atlanta Urban League from 1943 and in 1965 became the first African American woman elected to the Georgia General Assembly, representing a mid-Atlanta district for nearly two decades. She was a principal architect of Atlanta's 1973 city charter.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 1, "Twentieth-Century Residents", and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary" (H), entry "Hamilton, Grace Towns"

name: Rev. William Holmes Borders
bio: Pastor of Wheat Street Baptist Church from 1937 to 1988, Borders helped win the hiring of Atlanta's first Black police officers and led the 1957 bus protest that desegregated the city's buses. His church built Wheat Street Gardens, a church-run housing project for low-income residents.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), A Selected Biographical Dictionary, "B" (entry "Borders, William Holmes"); also ch. 1, "Twentieth-Century Residents", and ch. 13, "Stovall: 'In Gratitude'"

name: Rev. Fred C. Bennette Jr.
bio: A key SCLC organizer and aide to Martin Luther King Jr., Bennette coordinated the 1960 sit-in campaign to desegregate Rich's department store and was the first director of SCLC's Operation Breadbasket. He later advised Jimmy Carter and Andrew Young and directed security at the King Center.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), A Selected Biographical Dictionary, "B" (entry "Bennette, Fred C. Jr."); also ch. 1, "Twentieth-Century Residents"

name: Albert Hawes Watts
bio: Grandson of South-View co-founder Albert Watts, he began at the cemetery digging graves, became secretary-treasurer in 1948 and president-treasurer in 1977, and led it until his death. Henderson records he was the first African American on the American Cemetery Association board.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 3, "Albert Watts"; also ch. 4, "1940s – Sixtieth Anniversary" and "1970s – Ninetieth Anniversary"; ch. 6, "Twentieth-Century Cemetery Trends"

name: Jesse Hill Jr.
bio: Jesse Hill Jr. joined Atlanta Life Insurance Company as an actuary in 1949 and led it as president and CEO from 1973. He was the first African American member of the Georgia Board of Regents and the first Black president of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 1, "Historical Overview", section "Notable Twenty-First Century Residents"; and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary", H, "Hill, Jesse"

name: Dr. Asa G. Yancey Sr.
bio: Surgeon Asa G. Yancey Sr. was the first African American physician on staff at Grady Memorial Hospital and the first African American faculty member at Emory's medical school, where he started Georgia's first accredited surgical training program for African Americans.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 1, "Historical Overview", section "Notable Twenty-First Century Residents"; and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary", Y, "Yancey, Asa Greenwood"

name: Herman J. Russell
bio: Herman J. Russell bought his first property as a teenager and built his father's plastering business into H. J. Russell & Company, which helped build Atlanta landmarks such as the Georgia Dome. He also funded civil rights work and endowed entrepreneurship programs at Atlanta colleges.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 1, "Historical Overview", section "Notable Twenty-First Century Residents"; and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary", N - R, "Russell, Herman Jerome"

name: Mattiwilda Dobbs
bio: Atlanta-born coloratura soprano Mattiwilda Dobbs became the first African American to sing a principal role at Milan's La Scala in 1953. After her 1956 Metropolitan Opera debut as Gilda in Rigoletto, she became the first Black woman offered a long-term contract by the Met.

sources.label: D L Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), ch. 1, "Notable Twenty-First Century Residents", and "A Selected Biographical Dictionary" (D), entry "Dobbs, Mattiwilda"
